# Decision patterns, and a hybrid agent {#sec-ch12}

::: {.epigraph by="Alfred North Whitehead, 1911"}
Civilization advances by extending the number of important operations which we can perform without thinking about them.
:::

Cooks stop needing recipes once they see the few steps every recipe shares. Software has steps like that too, called **patterns**: common solutions with names. This chapter collects the patterns decision layers use, then builds an agent from them and races it against one where the LLM does everything.

![The six patterns in this chapter, as small diagrams. In every one, something else writes or acts, and a typed question decides.](/figures/ch22/catalog.pdf){#fig-catalog}

Every pattern shares one rule.

::: {.keyidea}
A decision model never writes and never acts on its own: it answers a typed question, and code acts.
:::

::: {.goals}
- Recognise six patterns for decision models in real systems.
- Find a decision step that's wrong without any error.
- Split work between a decision model and an LLM.
:::

## Six patterns

**1. Extract, then decide.** Input is messy (an email, a chat, a PDF) but the decision is small. LLMs read messy input superbly; they're weaker at the decision itself. So let the LLM turn the text into fields, and let a decision model decide from the fields. On our alerts, extracting first raised ranking (AUC) from {{< num ch22 llm_decides_auc f3 >}}, with the LLM deciding alone, to {{< num ch22 extract_then_jev_auc f3 >}}. But the security system's own structured fields scored higher still ({{< num ch22 jev_fields_auc f3 >}}): the alert text never mentions how critical the machine is or the user's job. No extractor can find a fact that isn't written down. So when structured data exists, use it.

![Extract, then decide. The LLM reads the raw text and writes structured fields; a decision model answers a typed question about them; policy thresholds turn the answer into an action. The LLM writes but never decides; the decision model decides but never writes.](/figures/ch22/extract.pdf){#fig-extract}

**2. The decide step.** An agent's loop is mostly small decisions. Give them to a decision model as typed questions, and call the LLM only when there's something to write. Because each decision comes with probabilities, the loop can notice when it's unsure and stop, instead of continuing confidently.

**3. The guardrail gate.** Before any risky action, ask a typed question about it using only *trusted* facts, never text an attacker could write. High probability allows the action, low blocks it, the middle asks a person: the three doors again, for actions instead of alerts.

![A guardrail gate. The agent proposes an action. A decision model estimates whether it's safe, from trusted facts only, never from text an attacker could write. High probability allows the action, low probability blocks it, and the middle asks a person.](/figures/ch22/gate.pdf){#fig-gate}

**4. Check the writer.** Some outputs must be written: an incident note, a customer reply. After the LLM drafts, ask typed questions *about* the draft: is every claim supported by the evidence? Is the tone right? Then send it, return it once for a rewrite, or give it to a person. Limit retries, or "write, reject, rewrite" never ends.

**5. The router.** Send each case to the right team with a pick-one question, but only automatically when the top option is clearly ahead. Routing every alert by its top label sent {{< num ch22 route_all_acc pct >}} to the right team; routing only when the top probability was at least {{< num ch22 route_line f1 >}} covered {{< num ch22 route_cov pct >}} of alerts and got {{< num ch22 route_acc pct >}} of those right. The rest went to a general queue. The same pattern can route between a cheap model and a slow one: Chapter 7's routing by doubt.

**6. The memory controller.** Agents keep notes and look things up, and each read and write is a small decision: is this worth remembering? Where should I look? A published system, Jev-Mem, uses a System One model for exactly these and calls a slow reasoning model only for the final answer; its authors report better answers and faster responses than the systems they compared [@jevmem2026]. Memory mistakes fail silently (a discarded fact just isn't there when needed), so log what gets thrown away.

## The hybrid agent

Now build Chapter 6's security agent as a **hybrid**: the decision model makes every decision, and the LLM writes only what a person will read. Every run leaves a **trace**, a step-by-step record of what was observed and what each decision said with what probability. It's a debugging tool, an audit log and an explanation in one.

![The hybrid agent. A cheap lookup always runs first. Jev decides which other evidence to collect, then answers the three verdict questions together. Chapter 14's policy turns the verdict into an action, and the LLM writes a case note or urgent message only when a person will read it.](/figures/ch24/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-17}

## The bug that didn't crash

When I first ran it over a live week, everything looked fine: no errors, every answer parsed, actions spread across the three doors. Then I ran a check worth running on every decision step of every agent: *count its answers*. Across {{< num ch24 n int >}} alerts, the "which evidence next?" step never once chose the threat-intelligence lookup, the most useful fact about an alert. Verdicts were reached without it, ranking dropped from {{< num ch24 v2_auc f3 >}} to {{< num ch24 v1_auc f3 >}}, and about {{< num ch24 v1_closed_threats_day f1 >}} real threats a day were auto-closed.

Typed answers always have the right format. The right format isn't the right answer, and nothing downstream will complain.

![How often the first version of the agent chose each option at its "which evidence next?" step, across 700 live alerts. It never once chose threat intel.](/figures/ch24/never-picked.pdf){#fig-never-picked}

::: {.keyidea}
Count every decision step's answers: an option never or always chosen is a warning, even without a crash.
:::

The fix wasn't a better model. A threat-intel lookup takes a fraction of a second and costs nothing; deciding *whether* to look it up costs about as much as just looking.

::: {.keyidea}
When looking is cheaper than deciding whether to look, don't decide. Just look.
:::

## Hybrid against all-LLM

The all-LLM agent runs the same loop, tools and thresholds; only who decides changes.

![Four measures for the two agents on the same 700 live alerts, scaled to a day. The LLM's stated confidences sent far more alerts to review than the queue can take, so more real threats were never seen by a person.](/figures/ch24/compare.pdf){#fig-compare-17}

The hybrid took {{< num ch24 v2_seconds f1 >}} seconds per alert; the all-LLM agent, {{< num ch24 llm_seconds f1 >}}. The bigger difference is the queue (@fig-compare-17). The LLM's written confidences cluster at a few round values, so the thresholds have almost nothing to separate, and it sent about {{< num ch24 llm_reviews_day int >}} alerts a day to a review queue that can take 240. The hybrid sent {{< num ch24 v2_reviews_day int >}}. A queue at twice capacity isn't worked twice as hard; the extra alerts just aren't seen. Counting threats closed unseen *and* never reached, the hybrid missed about {{< num ch24 v2_missed_day int >}} a day; the all-LLM agent, about {{< num ch24 llm_missed_day int >}}.

And where does the time go? The all-LLM agent spends most of it deciding. The hybrid spends its largest share *writing*: notes a person will read. That's where an LLM's time belongs.

![Share of each agent's total time spent on each kind of step. In the hybrid, the largest share is the LLM writing for people. In the all-LLM agent, most of the time goes on deciding.](/figures/ch24/labour.pdf){#fig-labour}

::: {.keyidea}
Use the LLM for the work only an LLM can do.
:::

::: {.breaks}
Everything here is synthetic, timings included, and part of the quality gap between the agents is built into the stand-ins. Treat the speed, the queue and the design lessons as the findings. And combining patterns adds failure points: an extractor feeding a gate feeding a router has three places to be wrong, and the errors multiply.
:::

::: {.exercises}
1. Design a guardrail gate for an email agent that can message customers. What's the typed question, which facts are trusted, and where do the thresholds go?
:::
